 3. Evaluation Criteria

 Responses to this RFR will be used to rank Applicants. As stated above, responses will not create any obligation by EEA to the responding parties. 3.1 Evaluation Components

 An EEA selection committee will review applications from responding organizations. Applications will be evaluated based, at a minimum, upon the following criteria:

 • Alignment with Program Goals (15%) Proposals will be assessed on how well they align with the program's overall objectives of reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and drought planning.

 • Project Impact (40%) Proposals must outline expected water savings, improvements in water loss control, and/or increased drought resiliency, with preference given to those that can deliver significant and measurable impacts. Proposals should outline clear, measurable outcomes and describe how project success will be monitored and evaluated.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

Examples of project types that are eligible include (but are not limited to): - Water Loss Control Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water loss control program development o Implementation of water loss control audit recommendations including distribution

 system leak detection activities and equipment meter calibration services/upgrades o Piloting or demonstrating new and innovative approaches (e.g. regional collaboration,

 new technology for leakage reduction and asset management) - Water Efficiency Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water conservation program/plan development and review of existing programs

 o Residential water use (rgpcd) and unaccounted-for water (UAW) compliance plan assistance

 o Data management and analysis assistance to inform water efficiency programs (e.g. compiling and analyzing use sectors and prioritizing largest users)

 o Residential leak detection activities (e.g. device incentive programs) o Public sector facility/municipal building upgrades to high-efficiency appliances/fixtures

 - Outdoor Water Use Efficiency Improvements o Drought resilient landscape design and/or implementation (i.e., conversions of irrigated

 turf to non-irrigated native plant landscapes, etc.) o Irrigation system audits (for functional turf areas) o Irrigation system upgrades to increase efficiency (for functional turf areas) o Drought resilient native plant demonstration/teaching gardens

 - Drought Management Planning o Bathymetric surveys, stage storage curve development, reservoir water level

 measurement implementation o Local drought plan development o Development of water use restriction programs

Examples of project types that are eligible include (but are not limited to): - Water Loss Control Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water loss control program development o Implementation of water loss control audit recommendations including distribution

 system leak detection activities and equipment meter calibration services/upgrades o Piloting or demonstrating new and innovative approaches (e.g. regional collaboration,

 new technology for leakage reduction and asset management) - Water Efficiency Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water conservation program/plan development and review of existing programs

 turf to non-irrigated native plant landscapes, etc.) o Irrigation system audits (for functional turf areas) o Irrigation system upgrades to increase efficiency (for functional turf areas) o Drought resilient native plant demonstration/teaching gardens

 - Drought Management Planning o Bathymetric surveys, stage storage curve development, reservoir water level

 measurement implementation o Local drought plan development o Development of water use restriction programs

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

THE COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS EXECUTIVE OFFICE OF ENERGY &

 ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS

 

 ONE HUNDRED CAMBRIDGE STREET SUITE 900, BOSTON, MA 02114

 

 Request for Responses (RFR)

 Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency Grant Program

 Project #: FY27EVRO0050 COMMBUYS #: BD-27-1042-ENV-ENV01-134023

 

 October 1, 2026Project #: FY27EVRO0050 | COMMBUYS #: BD-27-1042-ENV-ENV01-134023

 Page 1

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

SUBMISSION OF QUESTIONS: Written questions must be entered by pressing the “Bid Q&A” tab for the Bid in COMMBUYS no later than October 23, 2026. The issuing department reserves the right not to respond to questions submitted after this date. It is the Bidder’s responsibility to verify receipt of questions. At its discretion, EEA may publish answers to submitted questions via COMMBUYS (https://www.mass.gov/media/1455956/download - this is a .pdf file). If posted, EEA intends to post Questions and Answers on or before November 2, 2026. BUDGET REQUIREMENT: Applicants selected to receive grant funding will be required to submit documentation of expenditure for total approved project cost. PROJECT TERMS: If awarded, all projects will be required to abide by the Standard Commonwealth of Massachusetts Terms and Conditions. EEA does not guarantee that any contracts may result from this bid or that any particular funding level will be awarded. Only costs incurred during the contract period are eligible for reimbursement. CONTRACT DURATION: All contracts for grant assistance will end on or before June 30, 2027. All contracts will be delivered electronically for execution with a digital signature. DELIVERABLES: Grant recipients will be required to submit a brief Progress Report halfway through project completion and a Final Report following project completion. The progress report should include updates on key milestones, information on the implementation of project activities, and data demonstrating the impact of the project, including any measurable reductions in water use or improvements in water efficiency or loss control. The Final Report must supplement the Progress Report and also include an evaluation of project outcomes, lessons learned, recommendations for future efforts, and materials/language to support EEA outreach efforts related to the project. Lastly, grant recipients will be required to provide a brief presentation summarizing the project to the Massachusetts Water Resources Commission (WRC) or a separate forum, as applicable. Digital submissions must be provided in Microsoft Office compatible format or Adobe Acrobat and uploaded via the EEA Grant Management System (GMS). INVOICING: THIS IS A REIMBURSEMENT PROGRAM. Successful applicants will be required to execute a State Standard Contract prior to commencing work and will be required to manage their grant award contract, reports and reimbursement through the Grant Management System. Expenses incurred during the project may be reimbursed periodically. All reimbursement requests must use the form posted for this purpose in the GMS.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

THE COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS EXECUTIVE OFFICE OF ENERGY &

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

Organizations Involved and Regional Collaboration

Describe the individuals/organizations involved and any collaboration among municipalities, water suppliers, or nonprofits. Explain how the project will operate at a regional scale, if applicable.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

Examples of project types that are eligible include (but are not limited to): - Water Loss Control Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water loss control program development o Implementation of water loss control audit recommendations including distribution

 system leak detection activities and equipment meter calibration services/upgrades o Piloting or demonstrating new and innovative approaches (e.g. regional collaboration,

 new technology for leakage reduction and asset management) - Water Efficiency Program Development and Implementation

 o Comprehensive water conservation program/plan development and review of existing programs

 o Residential water use (rgpcd) and unaccounted-for water (UAW) compliance plan assistance

 o Data management and analysis assistance to inform water efficiency programs (e.g. compiling and analyzing use sectors and prioritizing largest users)

 o Residential leak detection activities (e.g. device incentive programs) o Public sector facility/municipal building upgrades to high-efficiency appliances/fixtures

 - Outdoor Water Use Efficiency Improvements o Drought resilient landscape design and/or implementation (i.e., conversions of irrigated

 turf to non-irrigated native plant landscapes, etc.) o Irrigation system audits (for functional turf areas) o Irrigation system upgrades to increase efficiency (for functional turf areas) o Drought resilient native plant demonstration/teaching gardens

 - Drought Management Planning o Bathymetric surveys, stage storage curve development, reservoir water level

 measurement implementation o Local drought plan development o Development of water use restriction programs

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

 3. Evaluation Criteria

 Responses to this RFR will be used to rank Applicants. As stated above, responses will not create any obligation by EEA to the responding parties. 3.1 Evaluation Components

 An EEA selection committee will review applications from responding organizations. Applications will be evaluated based, at a minimum, upon the following criteria:

 • Alignment with Program Goals (15%) Proposals will be assessed on how well they align with the program's overall objectives of reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and drought planning.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.

content.text:
By reducing the demand for water, communities can better preserve their water supplies during periods of drought and for fire protection, ensuring both the environment and the population have access to adequate water resources.

 Water efficiency measures such as upgrading infrastructure, installing efficient fixtures, and encouraging behavioral changes can significantly reduce the strain on water systems, particularly during peak demand periods. Outdoor water use, which often spikes in the summer months, can be a major contributor to water shortages, making conservation efforts in landscaping and irrigation systems vital to long-term water sustainability.

 At the same time, addressing water loss through implementing or improving comprehensive water loss control programs helps ensure that valuable water resources are not wasted. Many public water systems experience significant losses due to aging infrastructure, leaks, and inefficient operations. Tackling these losses not only helps conserve water but also improves the overall efficiency and resilience of the water supply network.

 The DRWE Grant Program seeks to fund innovative projects that promote climate resilience by helping communities and public water suppliers reduce both indoor and outdoor water use, improve water loss control programs, and increase drought management/planning. By supporting these efforts, the program aims to create lasting impacts on water conservation and drought preparedness, helping Massachusetts communities better adapt to the evolving climate and ensuring the sustainability of their water resources for future generations.

 1.3 Eligible Entities

 Eligible Entities include Municipalities, Public Water Suppliers, Nonprofit Organizations, Public Schools/Colleges/Universities, and Regional Planning Agencies. Partnerships between two or more entities are encouraged. We recognize that many water resource challenges, including drought management and water conservation, can often be addressed at a regional scale, where water systems and usage patterns often transcend municipal boundaries. Regional collaboration allows for a more holistic approach to water efficiency, as communities and organizations can pool resources, share best practices, and implement solutions that address broader watershed and regional water supply concerns. With this understanding, we are encouraging project proposals that incorporate regional-scale initiatives involving collaborations among multiple organization types, such as municipalities, public water suppliers, and nonprofit organizations.

 1.4 Compliance with Section 3A of MGL c. 40A (Zoning Act, MBTA Communities): 

 The receipt of grant funds is contingent upon the grantee being able to certify that it will comply with the Massachusetts General Laws, including G.L. c. 40A, § 3A, the MBTA Communities Act.

BUDGET REQUIREMENT: Applicants selected to receive grant funding will be required to submit documentation of expenditure for total approved project cost. PROJECT TERMS: If awarded, all projects will be required to abide by the Standard Commonwealth of Massachusetts Terms and Conditions. EEA does not guarantee that any contracts may result from this bid or that any particular funding level will be awarded. Only costs incurred during the contract period are eligible for reimbursement. CONTRACT DURATION: All contracts for grant assistance will end on or before June 30, 2027. All contracts will be delivered electronically for execution with a digital signature. DELIVERABLES: Grant recipients will be required to submit a brief Progress Report halfway through project completion and a Final Report following project completion. The progress report should include updates on key milestones, information on the implementation of project activities, and data demonstrating the impact of the project, including any measurable reductions in water use or improvements in water efficiency or loss control. The Final Report must supplement the Progress Report and also include an evaluation of project outcomes, lessons learned, recommendations for future efforts, and materials/language to support EEA outreach efforts related to the project. Lastly, grant recipients will be required to provide a brief presentation summarizing the project to the Massachusetts Water Resources Commission (WRC) or a separate forum, as applicable. Digital submissions must be provided in Microsoft Office compatible format or Adobe Acrobat and uploaded via the EEA Grant Management System (GMS). INVOICING: THIS IS A REIMBURSEMENT PROGRAM. Successful applicants will be required to execute a State Standard Contract prior to commencing work and will be required to manage their grant award contract, reports and reimbursement through the Grant Management System. Expenses incurred during the project may be reimbursed periodically. All reimbursement requests must use the form posted for this purpose in the GMS.

 3. Evaluation Criteria

 Responses to this RFR will be used to rank Applicants. As stated above, responses will not create any obligation by EEA to the responding parties. 3.1 Evaluation Components

 An EEA selection committee will review applications from responding organizations. Applications will be evaluated based, at a minimum, upon the following criteria:

 • Alignment with Program Goals (15%) Proposals will be assessed on how well they align with the program's overall objectives of reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and drought planning.

 • Project Impact (40%) Proposals must outline expected water savings, improvements in water loss control, and/or increased drought resiliency, with preference given to those that can deliver significant and measurable impacts. Proposals should outline clear, measurable outcomes and describe how project success will be monitored and evaluated.

 1. RFR Introduction and General Description 1.1 Description

 In recent years, the Commonwealth has been experiencing more frequent and intense drought. Since 2016, nine of the eleven years have had multiple months of drought. These droughts have caused impacts to water supply, habitat and the natural environment, and are exacerbating fire danger across the state. With climate change, increasing temperatures and predictions of more consecutive number of dry days, droughts are expected to increase in Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) is soliciting proposals from municipalities, public water suppliers, nonprofit organizations, public schools/colleges/universities, and regional planning agencies (RPAs) to participate in a Drought Resiliency and Water Efficiency (DRWE) Grant Program. The DRWE Grant Program aims to provide funding for projects that will help the Commonwealth become more climate resilient, specifically by reducing indoor and outdoor water use, improving water loss control, and increasing drought management/planning in communities and public water systems across the state. This is a REIMBURSEMENT program. Target awards are up to $50,000 per project. The program helps implement actions in the 2023 ResilientMass Plan.1 For the third year of this program, EEA has again adopted a relatively broad scope to encourage a diverse range of innovative proposals and is particularly interested in water efficiency and demand management projects that are not currently funded through other programs. The focus is on initiatives that promise the greatest long-term impact on water use reduction, ensuring sustainable water management for the future.
